title: Project Manager: Make a Status Update Clearer
summary: A B2 project manager can report completed work but loses control when explaining delays and dependencies.
studentContext: A B2 project manager leads a weekly remote status meeting with an international product team. The immediate goal is to explain progress, dependencies, and risk without reading a script.
evidence: The learner reports completed tasks accurately in a prepared update.
When a dependency causes a delay, the learner switches to vague phrases such as "there is a problem".
Homework used because and so correctly, but did not distinguish cause, consequence, and mitigation.
decisionReason: The core reporting skill is present, but the learner still needs support to explain cause, impact, and next action as one coherent update.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will deliver a 60-second status update that states a dependency, its impact, and one mitigation action without a written script.
activitySequence: Compare two short status updates and identify which one makes the dependency and impact explicit.
Rebuild three vague updates using the frame: dependency, impact, mitigation.
Rehearse one authentic project update with a keyword-only prompt.
Repeat the update after one follow-up question from the tutor.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the learner separates dependency, impact, and mitigation.
Whether the learner can respond to a follow-up question without returning to a full script.
Which linking phrases remain accurate under time pressure.

title: Software Engineer: Repair an Incident Explanation
summary: A B2 software engineer knows the technical content but uses an unclear timeline and ambiguous pronouns.
studentContext: A B2 software engineer needs to explain a production incident to a non-technical product manager. The learner understands the incident but must make the sequence and ownership clear.
evidence: The learner names the technical cause accurately.
The explanation jumps between detection, diagnosis, and recovery.
Repeated use of it and they makes the responsible system or team unclear.
decisionReason: The recurring timeline and reference errors block the listener from understanding the incident, so advancing to broader incident vocabulary would add complexity without fixing the communication failure.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will explain a four-stage incident timeline using explicit subjects and time markers that a non-technical listener can follow.
activitySequence: Order four incident events from detection to recovery.
Replace ambiguous pronouns with the system, service, or team responsible.
Explain the timeline once with a visual sequence and once without it.
Answer two non-technical clarification questions.
evidenceToCollect: Whether every event has an explicit actor or system.
Whether timeline markers remain accurate in the second explanation.
Whether clarification answers simplify rather than add technical detail.

title: Accountant: Advance From Variance Description to Recommendation
summary: A C1 accountant independently explains financial variances and is ready to add concise recommendations.
studentContext: A C1 accountant joins monthly calls with regional finance leaders. The learner can explain actual-versus-budget variance accurately and now needs to recommend a next action.
evidence: Two consecutive role-plays contained accurate variance language.
The learner used figures and comparison structures without tutor prompts.
No recurring language error changed the meaning of the explanation.
decisionReason: The previous objective is secure and independently transferable, so the next useful challenge is moving from explanation to recommendation.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will present one variance and recommend a proportionate follow-up action with a clear rationale.
activitySequence: Review a concise variance explanation and identify the missing decision.
Match three variance patterns with proportionate follow-up actions.
Prepare a 90-second recommendation from a short finance scenario.
Defend the recommendation against one challenge from a regional lead.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the recommendation follows logically from the stated variance.
Whether the rationale is concise enough for a finance call.
Whether the learner can adjust the recommendation after a challenge.

title: Lawyer: Continue Simplifying a Contract Risk
summary: A C1 lawyer identifies contract risk accurately but still relies on legal phrasing with clients.
studentContext: A C1 commercial lawyer advises startup clients in English. The immediate goal is to explain a limitation-of-liability risk without losing legal accuracy.
evidence: The learner identifies the relevant clause and consequence correctly.
The first explanation contains dense nominal phrases and long qualifications.
With tutor prompts, the learner can restate the point in shorter client-facing language.
decisionReason: The legal analysis is secure, but independent client-facing simplification is not yet stable.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will explain one contract risk in plain English, preserve the legal consequence, and check the client's understanding.
activitySequence: Separate the legal rule, practical consequence, and client decision.
Replace five dense legal phrases with precise plain-English alternatives.
Deliver a two-minute client explanation using a three-part structure.
Respond to a client who incorrectly paraphrases the risk.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the practical consequence remains legally accurate.
Whether the learner avoids unexplained legal nominalizations.
Whether the understanding check reveals and repairs a misunderstanding.

title: Sales Representative: Repair Follow-up Questions
summary: A B2 sales representative asks prepared discovery questions but misses information in the answer.
studentContext: A B2 sales representative runs software discovery calls. The learner has a reliable question list but needs to respond to the prospect's actual answer.
evidence: Prepared opening questions are accurate and natural.
The learner asks the next scripted question even when the prospect reveals a constraint.
Follow-up questions repeatedly use broad prompts that do not test the stated business impact.
decisionReason: Failure to build a relevant follow-up question blocks the purpose of a discovery call, so the next lesson should repair listening-to-question conversion.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will turn three prospect statements into specific follow-up questions about impact, urgency, or decision criteria.
activitySequence: Underline the decision-relevant detail in six short prospect answers.
Choose whether each detail requires an impact, urgency, or criteria question.
Run a branching discovery call in which the next prompt depends on the previous answer.
Review one missed opportunity and immediately replay that exchange.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the follow-up question reuses the prospect's meaning rather than a memorized script.
Whether the question type matches the information gap.
Whether the learner notices and repairs an irrelevant follow-up.

title: HR Professional: Continue a Performance Conversation
summary: A B2 HR professional can state a concern but needs more control when separating observation from interpretation.
studentContext: A B2 HR business partner supports managers during performance conversations. The learner must describe a behavior, its impact, and the expected change without sounding accusatory.
evidence: The learner can open the conversation and state the topic directly.
Examples sometimes mix observable behavior with assumptions about motivation.
The learner uses a neutral structure correctly after a model is provided.
decisionReason: The learner has partial control of the conversation structure but still needs scaffolding to keep evidence and interpretation separate.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will state one performance concern using observable evidence, impact, and a specific expected change.
activitySequence: Sort statements into observation, interpretation, impact, and expectation.
Rewrite three accusatory statements as evidence-based descriptions.
Conduct a short performance conversation with a resistant employee.
Repeat the difficult section using fewer tutor prompts.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the learner uses observable behavior rather than assumed intent.
Whether the expected change is specific and actionable.
Whether neutral language remains stable when the employee disagrees.

title: Marketing Manager: Advance to Defending a Campaign Recommendation
summary: A C1 marketing manager independently presents campaign evidence and is ready to defend a trade-off.
studentContext: A C1 marketing manager presents campaign performance to an executive team. The learner can describe results and recommend a channel allocation.
evidence: The learner independently summarized campaign results in two different data sets.
Recommendations used appropriate hedging and linked evidence to action.
No recurring accuracy problem remained in the target language.
decisionReason: The reporting and recommendation objective is secure, so the next lesson should add executive challenge and trade-off defense.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will defend a channel-allocation recommendation against two executive objections and state one condition that would change the decision.
activitySequence: Identify the strongest evidence and the weakest assumption in a campaign recommendation.
Prepare concise responses to cost, risk, and timing objections.
Present the recommendation to a skeptical executive role-play.
State a measurable condition for revising the allocation.
evidenceToCollect: Whether responses address the objection rather than repeat the original case.
Whether concessions preserve the central recommendation.
Whether the revision condition is measurable.

title: Consultant: Repair an Executive Summary
summary: A C1 consultant includes all analysis but does not prioritize the decision the client must make.
studentContext: A C1 management consultant gives five-minute project updates to a client steering committee. The immediate goal is to lead with the decision and support it selectively.
evidence: The learner's analysis is accurate and detailed.
The update starts with background and reaches the recommendation after several minutes.
This sequencing problem recurred in live practice and homework.
decisionReason: The repeated failure to foreground the decision blocks executive usefulness, even though the underlying English and analysis are strong.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will deliver a 90-second executive summary that starts with the required decision, gives two supporting facts, and names one risk.
activitySequence: Reduce a long update to decision, evidence, risk, and next action.
Compare background-first and decision-first openings.
Deliver three 30-second openings from different consulting scenarios.
Expand the strongest opening into a 90-second summary.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the required decision appears in the first two sentences.
Whether supporting facts are selected rather than listed.
Whether the named risk changes or qualifies the recommendation.

title: Entrepreneur: Continue a Customer Interview
summary: A B1 entrepreneur can ask about customer problems but still asks leading questions.
studentContext: A B1 founder interviews potential customers in English before building a product feature. The learner needs neutral questions that elicit past behavior.
evidence: The learner can explain the interview purpose and ask basic open questions.
Several questions suggest the desired answer or ask whether a proposed feature is useful.
After feedback, the learner can reformulate a leading question as a past-behavior question.
decisionReason: The interview structure is partially established, but neutral questioning is not yet independent enough to advance to complex probing.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will ask five neutral questions about a customer's last relevant experience and use one answer to ask a specific follow-up.
activitySequence: Identify leading language in eight customer-interview questions.
Convert feature-opinion questions into questions about the last real event.
Run a short interview using a one-page evidence grid.
Review whether each note records behavior, opinion, or assumption.
evidenceToCollect: Whether questions avoid suggesting a product or preferred answer.
Whether follow-ups refer to a concrete past event.
Whether notes separate observed evidence from the founder's interpretation.

title: Traveller: Advance From Routine Requests to Disruption Handling
summary: A B1 traveller independently handles routine hotel and transport requests and is ready for an unexpected disruption.
studentContext: A B1 adult learner is preparing for independent business travel. Routine check-in, directions, and simple requests are already secure.
evidence: The learner completed two routine travel role-plays without prompts.
Requests were polite, intelligible, and adapted to different contexts.
No recurring target error interfered with the outcome.
decisionReason: Routine travel communication is independently usable, so the next lesson should introduce a realistic disruption with negotiation and clarification.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will explain a missed connection, ask for two alternatives, and confirm the final arrangement.
activitySequence: Extract the essential facts from a missed-connection scenario.
Practice asking for alternatives and checking conditions.
Handle a role-play in which the first proposed solution is unsuitable.
Confirm the final route, time, and cost in the learner's own words.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the learner explains the problem concisely.
Whether at least two alternatives are requested or compared.
Whether the final confirmation catches a deliberately introduced misunderstanding.

title: Job Candidate: Repair an Achievement Answer
summary: A B2 job candidate describes responsibilities but does not show an individual result.
studentContext: A B2 operations specialist is preparing for an English job interview. The target question asks for an example of improving a process.
evidence: The learner describes the team and project context clearly.
The answer lists routine responsibilities but does not identify a specific action or measurable result.
The same gap appears in written preparation and spoken rehearsal.
decisionReason: The repeated absence of a specific action and result prevents the answer from demonstrating competence, so adding more interview questions would avoid the core problem.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will give a 90-second achievement answer that distinguishes the situation, personal action, and measurable result.
activitySequence: Mark team context, personal action, and result in two sample answers.
Select one authentic achievement and quantify the result conservatively.
Build a keyword outline with one sentence per function.
Answer the interview question twice, with a follow-up after the second version.
evidenceToCollect: Whether the learner uses I accurately for personal contribution.
Whether the result is specific without being exaggerated.
Whether the answer remains coherent after a follow-up question.

title: IELTS Candidate: Continue Developing One Task 2 Paragraph
summary: A B2 IELTS candidate has a relevant idea but needs support to develop it with explanation and evidence.
studentContext: A B2 adult learner is preparing for IELTS Writing Task 2. The current objective is paragraph development, not full-essay speed.
evidence: The topic sentence answers the prompt and states a clear position.
Supporting sentences repeat the main idea instead of explaining how or why it is true.
With a planning question, the learner can add a relevant example.
decisionReason: The paragraph has a valid controlling idea, but development still depends on prompts and does not yet justify advancing to full timed essays.
lessonObjective: By the end of the lesson, the learner will produce one Task 2 body paragraph with a claim, explanation, specific example, and explicit link back to the argument.
activitySequence: Diagnose repetition in two underdeveloped paragraphs.
Use how, why, and example prompts to expand one claim.
Write a paragraph from a four-part plan under a short time limit.
Revise one sentence that does not contribute to the argument.
evidenceToCollect: Whether each sentence has a distinct argumentative function.
Whether the example supports rather than merely illustrates the topic.
Whether the learner can plan the four parts without tutor prompts.
